name: Hormone bloodwork panel (total/free T, SHBG, E2, LH)

card.summary: The standard blood tests used to check testosterone status; clinical guidance exists, but interpreting free testosterone is technically contested.
card.note: Results depend on timing and assay method; interpretation belongs with a clinician.

quick.overview:
A hormone panel measures total testosterone, often free testosterone and SHBG, estradiol and LH. Clinicians use these tests to diagnose low testosterone and to tell primary from secondary hypogonadism.

In looksmaxxing circles it is described as the first step before any hormone-related plan.
quick.mechanism: Total testosterone is measured in blood, ideally in the morning. LH helps locate the cause: high in primary hypogonadism and low or normal in secondary. Free testosterone can be estimated or measured by equilibrium dialysis or mass spectrometry [1].
quick.risks: The test is a blood draw. The main caveats are interpretive: levels vary through the day, assays differ, and the free androgen index is considered a poor predictor of free testosterone [1].

lead: A hormone bloodwork panel typically measures total testosterone, free or bioavailable testosterone, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), estradiol (E2) and luteinizing hormone (LH). People use it to see what their hormones are actually doing before and while working on their physique, skin and hair, since these hormones influence muscle growth, body fat, oil production, hair growth and recovery [1][5].

Testosterone promotes muscle mass and strength, drives beard and body hair, enlarges sebaceous glands (which can mean oilier skin and acne), and is linked to male pattern hair loss in people who are genetically predisposed [5]. Estradiol and SHBG shape how much of that testosterone is available: only about 1 to 4 percent of circulating testosterone and estradiol is free, and a higher SHBG means less free hormone [4][5]. The panel gives people numbers to connect with how they look and feel.

Clinically, the panel is how low testosterone is identified, with LH checked to find the cause [1]. Endocrine Society guidance recommends diagnosing hypogonadism only in men with symptoms and consistently low testosterone, using a fasting morning total testosterone measurement as the first test [2].

chain: Blood test measures total and free testosterone, SHBG, estradiol and LH
Shows whether hormone levels sit in a typical range or point to a cause such as pituitary or testicular dysfunction
Informs decisions about training, body composition, skin and hair with a doctor
angle.text: The panel shows what lies behind changes in muscle gain, fat, energy, acne and hair, so people can discuss them with a clinician using measured values instead of guesses. It does not change appearance itself.

paras: Total testosterone is the amount in blood including protein-bound hormone. Most testosterone is bound to albumin or SHBG, and only a small free fraction is considered biologically active [5][4]. SHBG is a liver-made protein that binds androgens and estrogens; Wikipedia lists estrogen-rich states, hyperthyroidism and cirrhosis as raising it, and obesity, insulin resistance, hypothyroidism and androgens as lowering it [4].

LH is the pituitary signal that tells the testes to make testosterone. Primary hypogonadism usually shows elevated LH or FSH, while secondary hypogonadism shows normal or low levels [1]. Estradiol is measured because fat tissue converts testosterone to estradiol through aromatase [5].

The panel reflects a feedback loop. The hypothalamus releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone in pulses, the pituitary responds with LH, and LH stimulates Leydig cells in the testes to make testosterone. When blood testosterone is low the pituitary tends to release more LH, and as it rises, negative feedback suppresses GnRH and LH. Testosterone converted to estradiol also reduces LH pulse size. [9] This is why LH is read next to testosterone: a low testosterone with high LH is described as a testicular-origin pattern, and low testosterone with low or normal LH as a pituitary or hypothalamic pattern. [1][9] Because LH is secreted in pulses, a single sample can mislead, and levels may need to be followed over time. [9]

Most testosterone circulates bound: roughly two thirds to SHBG, about a third loosely to albumin, and only around 1.5 to 2 percent free, with free plus albumin-bound counted as bioavailable testosterone. [10] Estradiol in men is made largely by aromatase conversion of testosterone in fat and other tissues, with the testes supplying a smaller share. [11] Wikipedia gives a typical adult male estradiol range of about 14 to 55 pg/mL, notes that laboratories differ, and describes estradiol's role in bone health and in closing the growth plates. [11]

Wikipedia lists a typical adult male SHBG range of about 20 to 60 nmol/L, with pubertal males at 16 to 100 and women generally having about twice the male level. [4] About 33 to 70 percent of testosterone and estradiol is loosely bound to albumin, most of the remainder is tightly bound to SHBG, and only roughly 1 to 4 percent is free. [4] SHBG binds DHT most tightly, then testosterone, then estradiol, so changes in SHBG shift each hormone's free fraction differently. [4]

Factors listed as lowering SHBG include androgens and anabolic steroids, hypothyroidism, obesity, insulin, growth hormone and IGF-1, while estrogenic states such as oral contraceptives and pregnancy, hyperthyroidism, cirrhosis and anorexia nervosa raise it; long-term calorie restriction has been shown to raise it in rodents and men. [4] Low SHBG is linked to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. [4] A variant in the SHBG gene, rs6259, prolongs the protein's circulation and raises levels. [4] This is why trainees who change body weight, thyroid status or diet often see SHBG move and ask how it alters free testosterone.

Wikipedia's hypogonadism article lists, for men, impaired muscle and body hair development, gynecomastia, reduced height when onset is in youth, erectile dysfunction and sexual difficulties. Central causes may add headaches, visual disturbance or milk discharge, and hypogonadotropic forms may show late or absent puberty or lack of facial hair. [1] Testing may also occur during evaluation of delayed puberty or infertility. [1]

People who train, diet or manage hair and skin test hormones to connect symptoms they notice, such as stalled gains, fatigue, low libido, oily skin or acne, with measured values. Testosterone is linked to muscle, body hair and sebaceous gland activity, and in genetically predisposed people to pattern hair loss, so the numbers give context for those discussions with a clinician. [5] Estradiol, which Wikipedia describes as also affecting skin thickness and hydration, is checked because aromatase converts testosterone to it. [5][11]

People on prescribed testosterone therapy have the panel repeated during treatment, and the Endocrine Society guideline covers monitoring testosterone and other measures in men on therapy. [2] Others use it before and after changes such as weight loss, sleep changes or stopping a medicine.

Samples are usually drawn in the morning, because testosterone can fall by up to 13 percent over the day, and the Endocrine Society guideline recommends repeating a low result before diagnosis. [1][2] Test panels can be ordered through a physician or, in some regions, direct-to-consumer laboratories. Free testosterone may be reported as a calculated value from total testosterone, SHBG and albumin or as a directly measured one, and the choice of method affects the number. [3] Results are reported against each laboratory's own reference range. [11]

Guidelines cited by Wikipedia say a total testosterone below 300 ng/dL can support a diagnosis, treatment is often prescribed below 230 ng/dL with symptoms, and free or bioavailable testosterone should be checked for totals between 230 and 350 ng/dL [1]. Normal total testosterone generally ranges from about 240 to 950 ng/dL, and testosterone can drop up to 13 percent over the day, so reference ranges are based on morning samples [1].

An Endocrine Society position statement expressed dissatisfaction with most testosterone assays. Accurate free testosterone generally needs equilibrium dialysis or mass spectrometry, and the free androgen index is described as the worst predictor [1]. A 2019 review notes that measuring free testosterone is endorsed by recent clinical practice guidelines but remains debated, that assays are not harmonized, and that calculated free T equations are imperfect but can still give clinically useful results. It also says the free androgen index is not recommended in men because of inaccuracy at extremes of SHBG [3]. As of 2018 screening men without symptoms is not recommended [1].

Panels are a frequent topic on T Nation, where members compare free testosterone results, discuss unusual SHBG values and share bloodwork [6][7]. In one thread a member shared a family member's panel with high SHBG and low free testosterone and asked about options [7]. The threads mix personal results with opinion and are not clinical guidance.

The American Urological Association guideline (2018) states that the diagnosis can be supported by total testosterone below 300 ng/dL, and the Endocrine Society guideline of the same year recommends against screening men without symptoms. [1][2] The American College of Physicians issued testosterone-treatment guidance in January 2020 recommending annual reassessment for symptom improvement and discontinuation if there is none. [1] Earlier, a 2007 Endocrine Society position statement expressed dissatisfaction with most total, free and bioavailable testosterone assays, and a 2004 analysis characterised the free androgen index as the worst predictor of free testosterone. [1]

No studies found on the panel as a looksmaxxing practice. The Endocrine Society's 2018 guideline sets out how testosterone deficiency should be diagnosed with symptoms and repeated morning measurements [2]. A 2019 review summarises how free testosterone is assessed and the limits of each method [3]. A case report describes a man whose declining performance and low libido led to testosterone testing and eventual diagnosis of a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma, illustrating the panel's diagnostic use [8].

timeline.event: A published analysis describes the free androgen index, calculated from total testosterone and SHBG, as the worst predictor of free testosterone. [1]
An Endocrine Society position statement expresses dissatisfaction with most testosterone assays, including free and bioavailable measurements. [1]

The Endocrine Society publishes its testosterone therapy guideline for men with hypogonadism, and the American Urological Association guideline states total testosterone below 300 ng/dL can support diagnosis. [1][2]
A review states that free testosterone measurement is endorsed by recent guidelines but remains debated and that assays are not harmonized. [3]
The American College of Physicians issues testosterone treatment guidance recommending annual reassessment. [1]

lore.intro: On T Nation, members post hormone panels, ask what their numbers mean and compare free testosterone and SHBG values [6][7].

claims.claim: Free testosterone tells you more than total testosterone
claims.believers: Forum members compare free T and SHBG alongside total T, reasoning that a high total with high SHBG can still leave little free hormone [7].
claims.experts: A 2019 review says free T measurement is endorsed by recent guidelines but remains controversial, and that assays and calculations have limitations [3].

claims.claim: A hormone panel explains stalled progress in the gym or low energy
claims.believers: Members share bloodwork after plateaus or mood and energy changes and ask what the numbers mean [6].
claims.experts: The Endocrine Society recommends diagnosing hypogonadism only when symptoms and consistently low morning testosterone are both present [2].

claims.claim: The free androgen index is a quick way to estimate free testosterone.
claims.believers: Calculated indices from total testosterone and SHBG are easy to run from a standard panel, and members often compare such figures. [7]
claims.experts: The free androgen index is described as the worst predictor of free testosterone and is not recommended in men because of inaccuracy at extremes of SHBG. [1][3]

claims.claim: High SHBG means low usable testosterone even when total T looks normal.
claims.believers: Members point to high-total, high-SHBG, low-free-T patterns as an explanation for symptoms. [7]
claims.experts: SHBG governs how much testosterone is free, and guidelines suggest checking free or bioavailable levels when total testosterone is between 230 and 350 ng/dL. [1][4]
